parts.problem_md:
The number of outer-shell electrons in elements **X** and **Y** are 5 and 7 respectively.

What is the formula and the type of bonding in the compound formed between **X** and **Y**?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Both **X** (5 outer-shell electrons, Group 15) and **Y** (7 outer-shell electrons, Group 17) are non-metals.
- Neither element will transfer electrons to the other, as both strongly attract electrons to complete their octets. They must share electrons to form a **covalent** bond.
- **X** requires 3 more electrons to complete its octet, so it forms 3 covalent bonds.
- **Y** requires 1 more electron to complete its octet, so each **Y** atom forms 1 covalent bond.
- One atom of **X** therefore bonds with 3 atoms of **Y**, giving the formula **XY**<sub>3</sub>.

![Dot-and-cross diagram of a molecule with the structure of XY~3~, showing the central X atom with 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair](assets/001-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-a-molecule-with-the-str.jpg)

**A** and **B** are incorrect as the formula **X**<sub>3</sub>**Y** inverts the combining ratios. **X** needs 3 more electrons and forms 3 bonds, while **Y** needs only 1. One atom of **X** bonds with 3 atoms of **Y**, not the reverse.

**D** is incorrect as ionic bonding requires electron transfer from a metal to a non-metal. Both **X** and **Y** are non-metals with high numbers of outer-shell electrons. Neither element will donate electrons to the other, instead they must share them.

parts.problem_md: Which ion has a central atom with exactly three lone pairs of electrons?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Chlorine is in Group 17 and has 7 valence electrons.
- The 1− charge adds one electron, giving 8 available valence electrons on the central atom.
- Forming 2 bonds to the two fluorine atoms uses 2 of these electrons.
- The remaining 6 electrons on the central chlorine atom form **3 lone pairs**.

![Dot-and-cross diagram of ClF2- showing the central chlorine atom with 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs](assets/002-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-clf2-showing-the-centra.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as boron is in Group 13 (3 valence electrons). The 1− charge gives 4 available electrons on the central atom. Forming 2 bonds uses 2 electrons, leaving only 2 electrons / 1 lone pair on the central boron atom.

**C** is incorrect as phosphorus is in Group 15 (5 valence electrons). The 1− charge gives 6 available electrons on the central atom. Forming 6 bonds to the six fluorine atoms uses all 6 electrons, leaving 0 lone pairs on the central phosphorus atom.

**D** is incorrect as sulfur is in Group 16 (6 valence electrons). The 1− charge gives 7 available electrons on the central atom. Forming 5 bonds uses 5 electrons, leaving only 2 electrons / 1 lone pair on the central sulfur atom.

![Dot-and-cross diagrams of PF6-, BF2-and SF5- ](assets/003-dot-and-cross-diagrams-of-pf6-bf2-and-sf5.jpg)

parts.problem_md: Which statement about 2-chloropropene, CH<sub>2</sub>=C(Cl)CH<sub>3</sub>, is **not **correct?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The carbon atoms and the chlorine atom in 2-chloropropene all have 8 electrons in their outer shells, satisfying the octet rule.
- However, the five hydrogen atoms each have only 2 electrons in their outer shell when bonded to carbon. Hydrogen satisfies the duet rule (2 electrons), not the octet rule.
- Statement A is therefore incorrect as it is not true that every atom in the molecule obeys the octet rule.

![Structure of 2-chloropropene showing the C=C double bond, chlorine substituent, and hydrogen atoms](assets/004-structure-of-2-chloropropene-showing-the-c-c-dou.png)

**B** is not the correct answer as statement B is true. The C=C double bond consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond, so the molecule contains exactly one pi bond.

**C** is not the correct answer as statement C is true. The total number of valence electrons = (3 C x 4) + (5 H x 1) + (1 Cl x 7) = 12 + 5 + 7 = 24 valence electrons.

**D** is not the correct answer as statement D is true. Chlorine is in Group 17 and has 7 valence electrons. It uses 1 to form a single bond with carbon, leaving 6 non-bonded electrons, giving exactly 3 lone pairs.

choices.label: B

choices.text_md: The molecule contains exactly one π bond

parts.problem_md: Which molecule obeys the octet rule?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Carbon is in Group 14 and has 4 valence electrons.
- It uses all 4 to form two double bonds with the two sulfur atoms (S=C=S).
- This gives the central carbon atom **8 electrons** in its outer shell, a complete octet.
- Each sulfur atom also obeys the octet rule, with 4 electrons shared in the double bond and 4 in lone pairs.

![Dot-and-cross diagram of CS2 showing the central carbon atom with two double bonds and a complete octet of 8 electrons](assets/005-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-cs2-showing-the-central.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as beryllium is in Group 2 and has only 2 valence electrons. Forming 2 single bonds with chlorine gives the central beryllium atom only **4 electrons** in its outer shell, an incomplete octet.

![Dot-and-cross diagram of BeCl2 showing the central beryllium atom with only 4 electrons in its outer shell](assets/006-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-becl2-showing-the-centr.jpg)

**B** is incorrect as boron is in Group 13 and has 3 valence electrons. Forming 3 single bonds with fluorine gives the central boron atom only **6 electrons** in its outer shell, an incomplete octet.

![Dot-and-cross diagram of BF3 showing the central boron atom with only 6 electrons in its outer shell](assets/007-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-bf3-showing-the-central.jpg)

**D** is incorrect as phosphorus is in Group 15 and has 5 valence electrons. Forming 5 single bonds with chlorine gives the central phosphorus atom **10 electrons** in its outer shell, an expanded octet.

![Dot-and-cross diagram of PCl5 showing the central phosphorus atom with 10 electrons in an expanded octet](assets/008-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-pcl5-showing-the-centra.png)

parts.problem_md: Which species contains an atom with an incomplete outer shell?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Boron is in Group 13 and has 3 valence electrons.
- It uses all 3 to form single covalent bonds with the three fluorine atoms.
- This gives the central boron atom only **6 electrons** in its outer shell, which is in an incomplete octet.

**B** is incorrect as the carbon atom in CH<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> gains one electron from the negative charge, giving it 5 available valence electrons. It forms 3 bonds to hydrogen and has 1 lone pair, giving carbon a complete outer shell of 8 electrons.

**C** is incorrect as the oxygen atom in H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> loses one electron due to the positive charge, leaving 5 available valence electrons. It forms 3 bonds to hydrogen and has 1 lone pair, giving oxygen a complete outer shell of 8 electrons.

**D** is incorrect as magnesium oxide is an ionic compound. The magnesium atom transfers its 2 outer electrons to oxygen, forming Mg<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup>. Both ions have complete outer shells.

parts.problem_md: How many lone pairs of electrons are on the central atom in a molecule of chlorine trifluoride, ClF<sub>3</sub>?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Chlorine is in Group 17 and has 7 valence electrons.
- It forms 3 covalent bonds with the three fluorine atoms, using 3 of these electrons.
- The remaining 4 electrons on the central chlorine atom form 2 lone pairs.

![Dot-and-cross diagram of ClF3 showing the central chlorine atom with 3 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs in a T-shaped arrangement](assets/009-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-clf3-showing-the-centra.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 0 lone pairs would require all of chlorine's valence electrons to be used in bonding. Chlorine forms only 3 bonds, leaving 4 electrons as lone pairs.

**B** is incorrect as this applies the octet rule too strictly. Assuming chlorine needs only 8 electrons in its outer shell (3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair = 8) gives 1 lone pair. However, chlorine is in Period 3 and can expand its octet, so the correct count is 2 lone pairs.

**D** is incorrect as 3 is the number of lone pairs on each terminal fluorine atom, not on the central chlorine atom.

parts.problem_md:
Ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, reacts with a proton, H<sup>+</sup>, to form ammonium, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.

Using the following key:

•    N electron

$\times$   H electron

Which dot-and-cross diagram correctly illustrates the electron movement in this reaction?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The H<sup>+</sup> ion has no electrons to take part in the bonding with the ammonia molecule.

- The nitrogen atom has a lone pair of electrons that will form a dative (coordinate covalent) bond.

- A dative (coordinate covalent) bond is one where both electrons come from the same molecule.

**A **is incorrect as the arrow is showing nitrogen electrons moving from the hydrogen ion.

**C **is incorrect as there are no electrons shown.

**D **is incorrect as the diagram is showing hydrogen’s electrons moving from the nitrogen atom to the hydrogen ion.

parts.problem_md:
Calcium peroxide, CaO<sub>2</sub>, can be used in toothpaste as a teeth whitener.

Which dot-and-cross diagram represents the electron structure of the peroxide ion in CaO<sub>2</sub>?

![Dot-and-cross diagrams A, B, C and D showing different possible electron structures for the peroxide ion](assets/010-dot-and-cross-diagrams-a-b-c-and-d-showing-diffe.png)
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Calcium is in Group 2 and transfers its 2 valence electrons to form a Ca<sup>2+</sup> ion.
- The peroxide ion, O<sub>2</sub><sup>2-</sup>, consists of two oxygen atoms joined by a **single covalent bond**.
- Each oxygen atom is in Group 16 and has 6 valence electrons. One electron from each oxygen atom is used to form the O-O single bond.
- Each oxygen atom then receives one electron transferred from calcium to complete its octet, giving each oxygen atom 3 lone pairs.
- The correct diagram shows two oxygen atoms sharing one electron pair, with completed octets, enclosed in brackets with a 2- charge.

**B** is incorrect as this shows a double bond between the two oxygen atoms. This represents the neutral oxygen molecule, O<sub>2</sub>, not the peroxide ion. With a double bond, both oxygen atoms would have a complete octet without accepting any electrons from calcium.

**C** is incorrect as this diagram does not correctly represent the 2- charge of the peroxide ion. The O<sub>2</sub><sup>2-</sup> ion has received 2 additional electrons in total (one per oxygen atom). The electron arrangement shown does not match the single covalent bond plus completed octets required for the peroxide ion.

**D** is incorrect as this shows only a single oxygen atom. The peroxide ion contains two oxygen atoms joined together by a single covalent bond.

parts.problem_md: How many non-bonded, outer-shell electrons are present in one molecule of ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- There are no unbonded electrons in the hydrogens
- The nitrogen has 5 electrons on the outer shell, and shares 3 in total (one with each hydrogen)
- This leaves two unbonded electrons (a lone pair) on the outer shell of the nitrogen

![ammonia-dot-and-cross](assets/011-ammonia-dot-and-cross.png)

parts.problem_md:
Phosphorus tribromide and sulfur tetrafluoride are two colourless compounds which both react with water to form toxic products.

Draw diagrams to show the arrangement of outer electrons in both compounds.
parts.solution_md:
The dot-and-cross diagrams for phosphorus tribromide and sulfur tetrafluoride are:

Phosphorus tribromide (PBr<sub>3</sub>):

![Diagram of a phosphorus tribromide (PBr3) molecule, showing a central phosphorus atom bonded to three bromine atoms, with electron dot structures.](assets/012-diagram-of-a-phosphorus-tribromide-pbr3-molecule.bin)

Sulfur tetrafluoride (SF<sub>4</sub>):

![Dot-and-cross diagram of sulfur tetrafluoride showing a central sulfur atom bonded to four fluorine atoms, with one lone pair on sulfur and three lone pairs on each fluorine atom, demonstrating an expanded octet](assets/013-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-sulfur-tetrafluoride-sh.jpg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a correct dot-and-cross diagram of PBr<sub>3</sub>: central P atom with 3 bond pairs (one to each Br), 1 lone pair on P; 3 lone pairs on each Br atom
> 
> 1 mark for a correct dot-and-cross diagram of SF<sub>4</sub>: central S atom with 4 bond pairs (one to each F), 1 lone pair on S; 3 lone pairs on each F atom (expanded octet on S)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both PBr<sub>3</sub> and SF<sub>4</sub> have central atoms from Period 3, so they can accommodate more than 8 electrons in their outer shell (expanded octet). This is only possible for elements in Period 3 and beyond, because they have vacant d orbitals available.
> 
> For PBr<sub>3</sub>: phosphorus is in Group 15 (5 outer electrons) and each bromine is in Group 17 (7 outer electrons). Draw 3 bond pairs between P and each Br, plus 1 lone pair on P. Each Br has 3 lone pairs.
> 
> For SF<sub>4</sub>: sulfur is in Group 16 (6 outer electrons) and each fluorine is in Group 17 (7 outer electrons). Draw 4 bond pairs between S and each F, plus 1 lone pair on S (giving S 10 electrons in total). Each F has 3 lone pairs.

parts.problem_md: State the shape of, and the Br-P-Br bond angle in, a molecule of PBr<sub>3</sub>.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shape and bond angle of PBr<sub>3</sub> are:
> 
> - Pyramidal / trigonal pyramidal **[1 mark]**
> - 107° / approximately 107° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> PBr<sub>3</sub> has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central phosphorus atom. The lone pair exerts greater repulsion than a bonding pair, pushing the three P-Br bonds downward and reducing the bond angle from the ideal tetrahedral value of 109.5° to approximately 107°.
> 
> This is the same electron arrangement as NH<sub>3</sub>, PCl<sub>3</sub>, and NF<sub>3</sub>: all have a pyramidal shape and a bond angle of approximately 107°.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Phosphorus tribromide and sulfur tetrafluoride are two colourless compounds which both react with water to form toxic products.

Explain why molecules of PBr<sub>3</sub> and SF<sub>4</sub> are polar.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> PBr<sub>3</sub> and SF<sub>4</sub> are polar because:
> 
> - P-Br and S-F bonds are polar / there is a difference in electronegativity between the bonded atoms **[1 mark]**
> - The molecules have non-symmetrical shapes so the bond dipoles do not cancel **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both PBr<sub>3</sub> (pyramidal) and SF<sub>4</sub> (see-saw) have unsymmetrical shapes due to the lone pair(s) on the central atom. Even though each individual P-Br or S-F bond is polar, the key point is that the bond dipoles do not point in equal and opposite directions, so they cannot cancel.
> 
> Compare this with a non-polar molecule such as BF<sub>3</sub> (trigonal planar, no lone pairs). In BF<sub>3</sub> the three equal B-F dipoles cancel exactly because the molecule is perfectly symmetrical. The absence of lone pairs on the central atom is what allows full cancellation.

parts.problem_md: Construct an equation for the reaction of ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>, with a hydrogen ion.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the reaction is:
> 
> - NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sup>+</sup> → NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required

> **[exam-tip]**
> The ammonium ion, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, forms because the lone pair on the nitrogen atom in NH<sub>3</sub> is donated to the hydrogen ion. This forms a coordinate (dative covalent) bond between nitrogen and H<sup>+</sup>.
> 
> Note the → arrow: H<sup>+</sup> has no lone pairs to donate back, so this reaction does not proceed in reverse under these conditions.

parts.problem_md: Predict the shapes of an ammonia molecule and an ammonium ion.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shapes are:
> 
> - Ammonia: Pyramidal / trigonal pyramidal **[1 mark]**
> - Ammonium ion: Tetrahedral **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> NH<sub>3</sub> has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the nitrogen atom. The lone pair repels bonding pairs more strongly, compressing the H-N-H bond angle to approximately 107° and giving a pyramidal shape.
> 
> NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> has 4 bonding pairs and no lone pairs around nitrogen. All four pairs repel equally, giving a tetrahedral shape with a bond angle of 109.5°. The fourth N-H bond is a coordinate bond, but once formed it is identical to the other three.

parts.problem_md:
Draw a dot-and-cross diagram to show the bonding in the ammonium ion.

Show outer shell electrons only.
parts.solution_md:
The dot-and-cross diagram for the ammonium ion is:

![Dot-and-cross diagram of the ammonium ion showing a central nitrogen atom bonded to four hydrogen atoms, with three ordinary covalent bonds and one coordinate bond, enclosed in square brackets with a 1+ charge](assets/014-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-ammonium-ion-showin.jpg)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for 1 central nitrogen atom surrounded by 4 hydrogen atoms, with 3 shared pairs of electrons **AND** 1 coordinate bond shown with both electrons from nitrogen
> 
> 1 mark for square brackets **AND** 1+ charge outside the brackets

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two features are essential in this diagram:
> 
> - The coordinate bond:
> 
>   - Show both electrons using the same symbol (both dots or both crosses), donated from the lone pair on nitrogen.
>   - This distinguishes the dative bond from the three ordinary covalent bonds.
> - The ionic notation:
> 
>   - Draw square brackets around the complete ion and write the 1+ charge as a superscript outside.
>   - Without both of these, you will lose the second mark.

Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for the following molecules.

Show outer shell electrons only.

i) Hydrogen cyanide, HCN.

![Blank dot-and-cross diagram template for hydrogen cyanide showing the atom positions of H, C, and N with blank space for electrons](assets/015-blank-dot-and-cross-diagram-template-for-hydroge.png)

ii) Carbon dioxide, CO<sub>2</sub>.

iii) Boron trifluoride, BF<sub>3</sub>.

![Blank dot-and-cross diagram template for boron trifluoride showing the atom positions of B and three F atoms with blank space for electrons](assets/017-blank-dot-and-cross-diagram-template-for-boron-t.png)

parts.solution_md:
i) Hydrogen cyanide (HCN):

![Completed dot-and-cross diagram of hydrogen cyanide showing H bonded to C by a single bond and C triple-bonded to N, with a lone pair on nitrogen](assets/018-completed-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-hydrogen-cyan.png)

**[1 mark]**

ii) Carbon dioxide (CO<sub>2</sub>):

![Completed dot-and-cross diagram of carbon dioxide showing two double bonds from the central carbon to each oxygen atom, with two lone pairs on each oxygen](assets/019-completed-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-carbon-dioxid.png)

**[1 mark]**

iii) Boron trifluoride (BF<sub>3</sub>):

![Completed dot-and-cross diagram of boron trifluoride showing three single bonds from the central boron to each fluorine atom, with three lone pairs on each fluorine](assets/020-completed-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-boron-trifluo.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct HCN diagram: H single-bonded to C; C triple-bonded to N; lone pair on N only; correct electron counts throughout
> 
> 1 mark for correct CO<sub>2</sub> diagram: O=C=O with double bonds to each oxygen; 2 lone pairs on each O; no lone pairs on C; correct electron counts
> 
> 1 mark for correct BF<sub>3</sub> diagram: central B with 3 single bond pairs to three F atoms; 3 lone pairs on each F; incomplete octet on B (only 6 electrons around B)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each of these three molecules tests a different aspect of covalent bonding:
> 
> - HCN:
> 
>   - Carbon forms a triple bond with nitrogen (1 sigma + 2 pi bonds).
>   - Only nitrogen has a lone pair in the completed structure.
> - CO<sub>2</sub>:
> 
>   - Carbon forms two double bonds.
>   - Each oxygen has 2 lone pairs.
>   - Carbon has no lone pairs and a complete octet.
> - BF<sub>3</sub>:
> 
>   - Boron is in Group 13 and only has 3 outer electrons.
>   - After bonding to three fluorines, boron has only 6 electrons (an incomplete octet).
>   - This is why BF<sub>3</sub> acts as a Lewis acid and can accept a lone pair to form a coordinate bond.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for the following molecules.

Show outer shell electrons only.

i) Hydrogen cyanide, HCN.

ii) Carbon dioxide, CO~2~.

iii) Boron trifluoride, BF~3~.

Use your diagrams in (a) to deduce which of the three molecules is most likely to form a coordinate (dative covalent) bond. Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The molecule from (a) most likely to form a coordinate (dative covalent) bond is:
> 
> - Boron trifluoride (BF<sub>3</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - Boron's outer shell has space for two more electrons
> **OR**
> Boron only has six outer shell electrons / boron has an incomplete outer shell **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In HCN and CO<sub>2</sub>, the central carbon atom has a complete outer shell (8 electrons). It cannot accept an electron pair from a donor and so cannot form a coordinate bond.
> 
> In BF<sub>3</sub>, the central boron atom has only 6 outer shell electrons. This incomplete octet means boron can accept a lone pair from a donor molecule such as NH<sub>3</sub>, making BF<sub>3</sub> a Lewis acid. The coordinate bond forms when a lone pair is donated into boron's vacant orbital.

The molecule from (a) most likely to form a coordinate (dative covalent) bond is:

- Boron trifluoride (BF~3~)

Explanation:

OR

i) Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for the product of boron trifluoride and ammonia.

Show outer shell electrons only.

[1]

ii) Explain how the coordinate (dative covalent) bond forms between the boron trifluoride and ammonia molecules.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The dot-and-cross diagram for the product of boron trifluoride and ammonia is:

![Completed dot-and-cross diagram of the BF3-NH3 adduct showing a coordinate bond between the nitrogen atom of ammonia and the boron atom of BF3, with all outer shell electrons shown](assets/021-completed-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-bf3-nh3-a.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct BF<sub>3</sub>-NH<sub>3</sub> adduct: coordinate bond between N and B shown with both electrons from nitrogen using the same symbol (both dots or both crosses); correct lone pairs on all atoms
> 
> ii) The coordinate (dative covalent) bond forms because:
> 
> - Ammonia has a lone pair of electrons on nitrogen
> **AND**
> Boron trifluoride has an incomplete outer shell / only 6 electrons around B **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the dot-and-cross diagram of the product, the coordinate bond must be shown with both electrons from the same atom. Use two dots (from nitrogen's lone pair) between the N and B atoms, while the other N-H bonds each have one dot and one cross.
> 
> NH<sub>3</sub> acts as the electron pair donor (Lewis base) and BF<sub>3</sub> acts as the electron pair acceptor (Lewis acid). The lone pair from nitrogen fills the vacant orbital on boron to form the coordinate bond.

parts.problem_md:
Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for the nitrate(V) ion, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>.

Show outer shell electrons only.
parts.solution_md:
The dot-and-cross diagram for the NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> ion is:

![Dot-and-cross diagram of the nitrate ion showing a central nitrogen atom bonded to three oxygen atoms with one single covalent bond, one double covalent bond, and one coordinate bond, enclosed in square brackets with a 1- charge](assets/022-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-nitrate-ion-showing.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct bonding around N: one single covalent bond, one double covalent bond, and one coordinate bond to the three oxygen atoms; correct electron counts for each atom
> 
> 1 mark for square brackets **AND** 1- charge outside the brackets

> **[exam-tip]**
> The NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> ion has three different types of N-O bond. To construct the diagram:
> 
> 1. Start with nitrogen: 5 outer electrons.
> 2. Double bond: 2 electrons from N, 2 from O — this oxygen now has a complete octet.
> 3. Single bond: 1 from N, 1 from O — this oxygen needs 1 extra electron to complete its octet. That extra electron accounts for the 1- charge on the ion.
> 4. Coordinate bond: both electrons donated from N's lone pair to the third O atom.
> 5. Complete the lone pairs on each oxygen.
> 6. Enclose in square brackets and place the 1- charge as a superscript outside.
> 
> Without the square brackets and charge, you will lose the second mark.

parts.problem_md:
An ionic compound has the empirical formula H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.

Suggest the formulae of the ions present in this compound.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ions present in H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> are:
> 
> - NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> is the empirical formula of ammonium nitrate, NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>. One NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> ion and one NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> ion give the combined formula H<sub>4</sub>N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, confirming the match.
> 
> Learn the formulae and charges of all common polyatomic ions as CIE will not provide them. Key ions to know: NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>, SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>, CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>, OH<sup>-</sup>, and PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup>.
> 
> Always include the correct charge on each ion in your answer. Both the formula and the charge are required for each mark.

parts.problem_md:
Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for the CN<sup>-</sup> ion.

Show outer shell electrons only.
parts.solution_md:
The dot-and-cross diagram for the CN<sup>-</sup> ion is:

![Dot-and-cross diagram of the cyanide ion showing a triple bond between carbon and nitrogen, with a lone pair on carbon and a lone pair on nitrogen, enclosed in square brackets with a 1- charge](assets/023-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-cyanide-ion-showing.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct bonding: C≡N triple bond with correct electron distribution
> 
> 1 mark for the complete structure: lone pairs on both C and N **AND** square brackets **AND** 1- charge outside the brackets

> **[exam-tip]**
> The CN<sup>-</sup> ion has 10 outer electrons in total: 4 from carbon, 5 from nitrogen, and 1 extra for the 1- charge.
> 
> Distribute them as follows:
> 
> - Form a C≡N triple bond using 6 of the 10 electrons (3 shared pairs).
> - The remaining 4 electrons form 2 lone pairs: one on carbon and one on nitrogen.
> 
> Remember the ionic notation: square brackets around the complete structure with the 1- charge as a superscript outside. This is required for the second mark.

parts.problem_md:
Compare the C≡N bond energy and bond length in the cyanide ion, CN<sup>-</sup>, with the C-N bond energy and bond length in methylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>.

Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Comparing the C≡N bond in the cyanide ion with the C-N bond in methylamine:
> 
> - The bond energy of C≡N in CN<sup>-</sup> is greater than the bond energy of C-N in methylamine **[1 mark]**
> - The bond length of C≡N in CN<sup>-</sup> is shorter than the bond length of C-N in methylamine **[1 mark]**
> - CN<sup>-</sup> contains a triple bond whereas methylamine contains a single bond; a triple bond has greater electron density between the nuclei, requiring more energy to break **AND** pulling the nuclei closer together **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Bond energy and bond length are inversely related: the stronger the bond (higher bond energy), the shorter it is. Both trends have the same cause. More shared electron pairs between two nuclei means stronger electrostatic attraction, which pulls the atoms closer together and makes the bond harder to break.
> 
> The CIE 9701 definitions to know:
> 
> - Bond energy: the energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state
> - Bond length: the internuclear distance between two covalently bonded atoms
> 
> CIE 9701 uses the term bond energy (not bond enthalpy). Use the correct term in your answer.
